text: Book II of the *Republic* contains two arguments, and later readers have often treated them as separate projects. The first builds a city from scratch. Socrates presents it less as political theory than as a way of seeing the soul at a larger scale: the city is the person magnified, written in bigger letters so that justice can be read more easily (368d–369a). The second sets rules for what may be said about the gods (377e–383c), and here Plato was entering a quarrel already some two hundred years old. Homer and Hesiod were the closest thing Greece had to scripture, and their gods lied, lusted, fought their own kin, and handed out good and evil from two jars (*Iliad* 24.527–528). The philosopher Xenophanes had mocked those portraits in the sixth century BCE. In 399 BCE an Athenian jury condemned Socrates on charges of impiety and of corrupting the young. Plato answers by making the founders of his city theologians before they are lawgivers. They decide what a god must be before they decide what children may hear. The founding premise of the whole construction is that a city is a remedy for human neediness. Aristotle would later dispute that premise and hold that the city is something natural to human beings.
